item.title: Russia is developing a nuclear space weapon, US intelligence report finds
item.description: null Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space. The new report focuses on China , Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon . The report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain . Information within the report, which you can read here , is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought. Up-front finding The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits." Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations. The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites , which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security." While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests. There are a range of threats to space-based services, both commercial and military. Some are reversible, while others are not. (Image credit: DIA) Counterspace worries A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen. Counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system. Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report: Antisatellite (ASAT) missiles are designed to kinetically strike and destroy satellites. ASAT missiles could produce massive amounts of debris that can remain in orbit for decades or even centuries. Physical or cyberattacks against ground sites and other terrestrial infrastructure supporting space operations can also threaten satellite services. Cyber counterspace attacks target the satellite data within the transmission signal, along with the systems that use, transmit and control the flow of data. Electronic at
item.dc:creator: Leonard David
item.content:encoded: null Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space. The new report focuses on China , Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon . The report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain . Information within the report, which you can read here , is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought. Up-front finding The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits." Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations. The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites , which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security." While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests. There are a range of threats to space-based services, both commercial and military. Some are reversible, while others are not. (Image credit: DIA) Counterspace worries A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen. Counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system. Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report: Antisatellite (ASAT) missiles are designed to kinetically strike and destroy satellites. ASAT missiles could produce massive amounts of debris that can remain in orbit for decades or even centuries. Physical or cyberattacks against ground sites and other terrestrial infrastructure supporting space operations can also threaten satellite services. Cyber counterspace attacks target the satellite data within the transmission signal, along with the systems that use, transmit and control the flow of data. Electronic attacks include jamming and spoofing techniques to target a nation's use of the electromagnetic spectrum. Electronic attacks can interfere with systems used for communications and command and control of military forces, including piloted and unpiloted vehicles. Directed-energy weapons (DEWs) can temporarily or permanently blind image-collecting satellites and affect overhead persistent infrared and weather sensors, thereby denying the ability to monitor, track and target forces. 'Boom time' in space? The DIA report underscores that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon . Russia is doing so despite its obligation to comply with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty . That U.N. agreement prohibits the placement of any objects carrying nuclear weapons, or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, into orbit around Earth. "A space-based capability such as this could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by countries and companies around the world," the DIA report states, "as well as to the vital communications, navigation, scientific, meteorological, commercial and national security services they provide." A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits, the DIA report warns, from low Earth orbit for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, geosynchronous orbit for critical communications, and medium Earth orbit for navigation and timing satellites. This graphic identifies the various destinations for spacecraft relatively close to Earth, including cislunar space. (Image credit: DIA) Cislunar developments The newly issued DIA report also observes that exploring cislunar space is of increasing interest to spacefaring nations for potential scientific and economic opportunities. However, nations such as China "may be exploring military applications from cislunar space," the report notes. China has stated its goal of developing a cislunar space economy by 2045. "China is also the first country to attempt sustained operations on the far side of the moon , with numerous projects slated to support that effort through the next decade. China portrays its interest in cislunar space as peaceful, but PRC [People's Republic of China] officials have also discussed pursuing military capabilities in cislunar space," the report states. DIA appraisals Placing a keen eye on the DIA report is Peter Garretson, a senior fellow in defense studies at the American Foreign Policy Council and a strategy consultant who focuses on space and defense. According to Garretson, the most significant positive change from earlier DIA appraisals is the explicit assessment that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. He told Space.com that the DIA's expanded treatment of the threat of a nuclear weapon on orbit reflects concerns in the Congress and the Trump White House. However, Garretson also flagged what he said is a consequential omission in the report: the disappearance of the prior treatment (in the 2022 version of the report) of research competition, surveillance beyond geosynchronous Earth orbit and the potential military use of deep space for staging reserve forces. Puzzle pieces In Garretson's view, the DIA needs to help put the puzzle pieces together for Congress and the attentive public about what exactly China is doing, and how it fits together in the nation's strategy to achieve comprehensive space dominance. According to Garretson, "everything they are doing, from launch cadence, reusable launch, commercial space investment, investments in power, propulsion, repair, manufacturing, to commercial assets working together" supports both an economic expansion toward new resources and what China hopes will be overwhelming military power and strategic depth. China's mysterious Shenlong space plane, imaged by a Vantor satellite in Earth orbit. (Image credit: Satellite image ©2026 Vantor) Outlook for the future Garretson senses the moves by China to develop extractive and in-space industries "is truly the strategic threat that could crush American space power. Now is the time to be making the investments to ensure we have a 'freedom's forge' and 'arsenal of democracy' in space that can protect the open space commerce that is the nation's strategy." As for the DIA's outlook for the future: The agency concluded that space almost certainly will remain an increasingly competitive and crowded environment as space capabilities improve and other countries seize opportunities in the final frontier. "The increase of Chinese, Russian, Iranian and North Korean counterspace capabilities, rapid growth in the number of space objects, and the proliferation of requirements for space-enabled services," the DIA report states, "will all complicate operations in space in the coming decade."

item.title: Dutch data watchdog highlights safety issues with AI glasses
item.description: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities. The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor. In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call. Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events. The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role." A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense. "Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP. "AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified." The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary. The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI. The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured. On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera. Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.” Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable. item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) has officially advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses after safety tests revealed concerning behaviors beyond their controversial recording capabilities. The AP recently tested six different models of smart glasses and found glaring issues, including a willingness to display dating advice to an adult glasses-wearer who expressed an interest in a minor. In another case involving a cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) simulation, testers noted that one pair of glasses informed the wearer that emergency services had been called and were scheduled to arrive at the scene, despite no one having made the call. Some glasses did not properly process safety warnings on children’s toys, others made mistakes when reading medication leaflets, and some misinterpreted warnings for extreme weather events. The AP did not specify the models it tested, saying only that they tested six models ranging from under €100 ($110) to over €500 ($550), including two that "were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations where human safety played a key role." A spokesperson also declined to match any specific behavior to a model by price point (minor dating advice linked to a €354 pair of glasses, for example), adding that the research was intended to highlight the risks of AI glasses in a broader sense. "Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning. Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone's life is at stake go a step too far," said Monique Verdier, vice chair at the AP. "AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified." The warning issued this week follows the regulator's previous work on smart glasses. The AP reminded the public in September that everyone has the right to privacy and encouraged organizations to ban them where necessary. The same warning mentioned the potential risks regarding data processing under the GDPR, as well as those related to the training of AI. The AP doubled down on these earlier criticisms, saying the latest tests showed that the AI functions rely on processing data using servers mostly located outside of the European Union. Relatedly, it found that users were not given sufficient information about how the AI was processing the data they captured. On a cybersecurity note, the tests threw up a range of issues, including the ability for people nearby the glasses-wearer to connect to the device without permission, view recordings, and in some cases operate the camera. Further, the regulator echoed the pre-existing concerns about smart specs - those that helped give them their colloquial name “pervert glasses.” Its tests found that with "virtually all of the camera glasses examined," the recording lights that are supposed to clearly show when a user is recording were dim and easily coverable. The AP said that models could also be wangled into recording even when that light indicator was covered, which goes against what manufacturers so often claim. "As a result, bystanders can barely see whether they are being filmed," it said. The technology has a number of beneficial use cases, such as assisting the visually impaired, those with lower literacy levels, or for any number of other scenarios where people need help understanding the world around them However, the watchdog's official stance on the technology, as it is today, deems smart glasses "unsafe… due to the risks to users and bystanders." Verdier said politicians in the Netherlands and across Europe should take note of the results when developing AI policy. "It is important that we, as a society, learn to deal with these types of high-risk AI products," she said. "Simply banning everything provides some leeway in the beginning, but we cannot sustain that indefinitely. It is important that we collectively work on awareness, resilience, and ethical conscience." Smart specs can't shake the hate When DEF CON announced a no pervert glasses policy ahead of its event in August, the move was broadly welcomed by attendees. "Love to see a ‘no pervert glasses’ policy at DEF CON," said Eva Galperin, EFF director of cybersecurity, at the time. Several other organizations have implemented similar restrictions, including Monopoly Events, which manages UK Comic Cons, national treasure pub chain Wetherspoons , and even Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Most members of the general public will have at least come to terms with the fact that the smartphone generation, and their willingness to snap shots anywhere and everywhere, means there is no enshrined human right to privacy in public spaces. Public video recording once carried an air of expectation or consideration for bystanders’ personal privacy, although smartphone users have slowly eradicated that over time. Like it or not, it's generally understood that a smartphone is usually recording something - or someone - at any given time, especially in urban areas. On paper, the fact that smart glasses can record in public spaces isn’t wildly different from what’s already come to be expected from smartphones. However, given how similar they appear to analog glasses and the ability to cover the recording light, it makes the act of public recording via glasses far more surreptitious, and thus concerning. With smartphones, it's easy to see from the user's body language - holding the phone out in front of them - that they are recording. There are no overt signals displayed by wearers of smart glasses during image or video capture, which fuels a sense of unease about the technology in general. A quick search online for "smart glasses privacy violation" yields a slew of complaints about the technology, often regarding behavior toward women and children. There are also worries about how easily the devices can get past security checks, potentially providing opportunities to those who wish to cause greater harm than a mere blight on personal privacy. A joint investigation by The Observer and BBC Radio 4 recently revealed how AI-enabled glasses went undetected through the airport-style security scanners used in the UK parliament. The two news outlets found that a £60 ($78) pair of Chinese-made glasses bypassed the scanners and could be used to read upside-down documents on MPs' desks, recording data such as phone numbers and addresses to be accessed at a later point. ®

item.title: France investigates actor Depardieu, writer Houellebecq over alleged gang rape
item.description: French police are investigating allegations actor and convicted sex offender Gérard Depardieu raped and assaulted a woman with the complicity of bestselling author Michel Houellebecq during a 2018 film shoot, two sources following the case said Friday. The plaintiff has accused the film's director Guillaume Nicloux of being complicit in the abuse.

NASA/Danny Nowlin Employees contributing to NASA’s mission at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, were recognized during the center’s Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18. Presenting the awards were Christine Powell, NASA Stennis center director, and Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager responsible for management and oversight of NASA’s initiative to return humans to the Moon. Stephen Rawls of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Center Director’s Excellence Award for exceptional leadership and technical excellence in advancing NASA Stennis propulsion testing capabilities for critical NASA and commercial programs. Bradley Tyree of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Engineering Excellence Award for engineering excellence and contributions to the successful testing of the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment Confined by Missile Program. Anna Lizana of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Excellence in Customer Service Award for exceptional environmental compliance support that advanced commercial partnerships, streamlined agency processes, and reduced regulatory risk. Daniel Jones of Huntsville, Alabama, received the Excellence in Innovation Award for the invention of the Hydrocarbon Propellants Enabling Reproduction of Flows in Rocket Engines, a system for low-cost aerodynamic data acquisition. Peyton Pinson of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Leadership Excellence Award for exceptional leadership as E-1 test director, providing steady guidance and strengthening team cohesion throughout a demanding and high-tempo year of propulsion testing. Joseph Schuyler of Pass Christian, Mississippi, received the J. Harry Guin Leadership Award for transformative leadership that advanced NASA Stennis propulsion testing capability and strengthened its role as the agency’s Center of Excellence in Propulsion Testing. Michael McDaniel of Slidell, Louisiana, received the Roy S. Estess Service Leadership Award for exceptional partnership, sustained leadership, and an unwavering commitment to his community as the general manager of L3Harris Technologies at NASA Stennis that embodies the legacy of the late center director. Amer Arshad of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Space Flight Awareness Trailblazer Award for innovative leadership, system stewardship, and collaborative solutions that have strengthened NASA’s mission through improved reliability, insight, and efficiency. Claire O’Shaughnessy of Mandeville, Louisiana, received the Space Flight Awareness Trailblazer Award for innovative leadership and collaborative drive that strengthened the center’s mission by advancing critical facility capabilities for the agency’s Artemis program. In addition to individual awards, the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment, Confined by Missile Test Team received the Space Flight Awareness Team Award for exceptional technical achievement in executing a test series that has provided mission critical safety data for the future of human spaceflight. Briou Bourgeois accepted the award on behalf of the team, which included: Chase Aubry, Brandon Carver, Jack Conley, James Connell, Armando Delgado, Mateo Ferreira, Pau Fuller, Mark Hancock, Steven Helmstetter, Paula Hensarling, Jason Hopper, Chase Lemaire, Addison Mitchell, Randall Pigott, Stephen Rawls, Skip Roberts, Mark Robinson, Luke Roger, Matthew Sappington, Robert Simmers, Jason Richard, Bradley Tyree, Richard Wear, and Robert Williams. The ceremony also honored employees who reached significant milestone anniversaries in their civil service careers. Employees with 40 years of service were Curtis Armstrong, Jason Edge, and Kevin Power. Employees with 35 years of service were Michael Brashear, Reginald Ellis II, Arlen Griffey, Bradley Messer, Christine Powell, and Michael Rewis. Skip Roberts was recognized for 30 years of service. Employees with 25 years of service were Gregory Carmouche, Thomas Carroll, Craig Chandler, Jorge Figueroa, Jared Grover, Melissa Huggins, Scott Jensen, Jeffrey Lott, Christopher Mulkey, Richard Rauch, Ryan Roberts, Karen Seals, Joseph Schuyler, Peterve Tran, and Maury Vander. item.title: Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION
item.description: If you're wondering how Alex Ridha's (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION , the answer is simple: It didn't. That's not to say Ridha didn't learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but most of the songs on 7LLVSION had been knocking around for some time. And as Ridha is quick to point out, these are not rock songs built for live performance; they're "battle tested" for clubs and DJ sets. "I was kind of back on the usual kind of thing," he tells The Verge . "I do the same I kind of always do. item.title: Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines
item.description: When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June , Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn't secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change. "We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels," Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday . "As a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained." If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025 , with additional price hikes happening this year. Read full article Comments

item.title: AI boom threatens circuit board crunch to rival pandemic-era chip shortage
item.description: The electronics industry faces a printed circuit board (PCB) shortage that could rival the pandemic-era chip crunch – with AI once again accused of hogging supplies. The Global Electronics Association says demand is arriving "at a scale the supply chain was not built for," straining everything from glass fabric and resin to finished boards. Its report, " The PCB Squeeze: A Wake-Up Call for Global Electronics ," says AI servers need increasingly complex boards. While a typical PC board has about 12 layers of tracks, AI server boards can have 40 to 60 layers or more, and each additional layer requires more resin, copper foil, and laminate. The supply of materials is set to be constrained through at least the first half of 2027, the report says, with meaningful relief unlikely before mid-2028. Programs to deliver PCBs for automotive, industrial, medical and even the defense industries are being crowded out as AI soaks up scarce capacity, it claims. The association's North American figures show orders growing much faster than deliveries. PCB bookings rose 56.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while PCB shipments increased 13.3 percent. Fabrication capacity is expanding, aimed at meeting the increased demand from the AI infrastructure sector, especially in Asia, where more than 90 percent of the world's boards are made. The report says that $10 billion has gone toward new PCB plants in Southeast Asia, and at least as much has been invested in China over the past three years, but the raw materials are themselves constrained. It warns of lengthening lead times for those raw materials. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three weeks a year ago, while advanced low-loss laminates now take 14 to 18 weeks for delivery, for example. Tightening supplies usually lead to price increases, and the report says that suppliers raised laminate costs by 30 percent in September, and that the price tag of some types of E-glass cloth for circuit boards has risen by 300 percent. The report also puts copper prices up 37 percent over the past year. Concerns have been raised about copper supplies before, as The Register has reported multiple times. The association compares the risk with the 2021 chip shortage , when disrupted supplies left manufacturers unable to secure even relatively mundane components. New capacity is coming, but it is late and comes in dribs and drabs, according to the report, while AI demand just keeps on absorbing it as soon as it arrives. The association's advice is for buyers to plan early, and to share realistic forecasts with suppliers rather than double-booking. Board makers should qualify alternative suppliers of materials such as laminate and copper foil before shortages bite, but it warns against stockpiling beyond real need, which adds to forward-buying pressure. But it would like governments to step in, of course, by tracking board and material lead times

Programs to deliver PCBs for automotive, industrial, medical and even the defense industries are being crowded out as AI soaks up scarce capacity, it claims. The association's North American figures show orders growing much faster than deliveries. PCB bookings rose 56.1 percent in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year, while PCB shipments increased 13.3 percent. Fabrication capacity is expanding, aimed at meeting the increased demand from the AI infrastructure sector, especially in Asia, where more than 90 percent of the world's boards are made. The report says that $10 billion has gone toward new PCB plants in Southeast Asia, and at least as much has been invested in China over the past three years, but the raw materials are themselves constrained. It warns of lengthening lead times for those raw materials. Standard FR-4 laminate now takes six to eight weeks to ship, up from two to three weeks a year ago, while advanced low-loss laminates now take 14 to 18 weeks for delivery, for example. Tightening supplies usually lead to price increases, and the report says that suppliers raised laminate costs by 30 percent in September, and that the price tag of some types of E-glass cloth for circuit boards has risen by 300 percent. The report also puts copper prices up 37 percent over the past year. Concerns have been raised about copper supplies before, as The Register has reported multiple times. The association compares the risk with the 2021 chip shortage , when disrupted supplies left manufacturers unable to secure even relatively mundane components. New capacity is coming, but it is late and comes in dribs and drabs, according to the report, while AI demand just keeps on absorbing it as soon as it arrives. The association's advice is for buyers to plan early, and to share realistic forecasts with suppliers rather than double-booking. Board makers should qualify alternative suppliers of materials such as laminate and copper foil before shortages bite, but it warns against stockpiling beyond real need, which adds to forward-buying pressure. But it would like governments to step in, of course, by tracking board and material lead times with industry and offering tax incentives for investment in advanced PCB and substrate manufacturing equipment. The wish list also includes state investment in research and development plus qualification of new alternative materials. It would like to see loan guarantees and grants to protect critical programs and small fabricators, structured so as to sustain new capacity if forward buying unravels and demand corrects in 2027. "Yes, we are seeing constraint in upstream materials and have been reporting it for the past couple of quarters," said Cori Masters, senior research analyst director for Supply Chain Operations at Gartner. "In addition, AI datacenter infrastructure build out is moving capacity support to high-layer count PCBs which increase throughput time and decreases availability of line utilization for more traditional PCB products," she told The Register . ®

item.title: Asali Africa: Serves Up ‘There’s Rice at Home’ A New Cooking Series Hosted by Chef Soliat Bada
item.description: Chef Soliat Bada Anyone who grew up in a Nigerian home knows the line. You suggest buying food outside, and before you finish the sentence, someone reminds you that there’s rice at home. It is usually the end of the conversation. In Asali Africa’s new series, it is where the conversation starts. There’s Rice at Home is a cooking and conversation show from Asali Africa, the Lagos-based creative development agency, hosted by Chef Soliat Bada . In each episode, Soliat cooks one rice dish with a guest, and while the pot does its work, the two get into the kind of talk that usually happens around food: family, money and what success really looks like. Rice is the most ordinary thing in a Nigerian kitchen, and the show makes a good case that it doesn’t have to taste ordinary. Over five episodes, released every two weeks, the menu travels from Jamaica to Saudi Arabia, back home to Nigeria and on to Louisiana. You don’t just watch the food get made, either. The recipes are written up in full on Asali Africa’s website, with the ingredients and method laid out step by step, so you can watch Soliat cook a dish and then make it in your own kitchen. The season opens with Rice and Peas with Oxtail, the Jamaican Sunday staple of rice cooked in coconut milk with red kidney beans (the “peas”), served beside rich, slow-cooked oxtail. Soliat’s guest is Michael Famoroti , co-founder of Stears, and their conversation turns to family and black tax: the expectation that once you start earning, you start supporting the people who raised you. Read the full recipe for Rice and Peas with Oxtail . Rice and peas with oxtail, from Episode 1 Soliat Bada and Michael Famoroti in Episode 1 Episode 2 moves to the Gulf for lamb kabsa, Saudi Arabia’s national dish, fragrant with dried lime and seven spice. Soliat is joined by Bella Adeleke , CEO of Asali Africa and founder of the fashion label Garbe, for a conversation about redefining success. Read the full recipe for Lamb Kabsa . Lamb kabsa, from Episode 2 Still to come are Nigerian fried rice with fried turkey and dodo, cooked with Toyin Jolapamo and Nneoma Mere; jambalaya with Goldie Iyamu and Vanessa Iloenyosi ; and a season finale with Edwin Okolo and Temi Omolehinwa. For more on Asali Africa and the products and ideas it develops, visit asali.africa . Episodes 1 and 2 are out now on YouTube. Watch Episode 1 below. https://www.youtube.com/embed/-6Ux0-vNDnw Sponsored Content The post Asali Africa: Serves Up ‘There’s Rice at Home’ A New Cooking Series Hosted by Chef Soliat Bada appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
item.description: The Riemann hypothesis describes a pattern within the prime numbers ROBERT BROOK/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Alamy A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics. The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution. Read more OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI. Advertisement “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis , but that stopped short of a full proof. Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages. Instead, Alpöge has released a version of the proof written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. This process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning that the code compiles, it is considered to have been proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt. However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.” A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now

However, the process isn’t without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. “Let’s see if it compiles first,” says Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, reacting to the news. “Might be a while before we find the relevant experts who are able to tell us the thrust of the argument, assuming it’s all true, of course, which it probably will be because of course Alpöge will have [a] huge amount of egg on [his] face if the Lean code doesn’t compile or is deficient in some way.” A golden age of maths is dawning and mathematicians are freaking out Mathematicians are stunned at the progress AI is making in solving advanced problems, leaving some questioning whether there will still be room for humans Alpöge says the proof may also help solve the generalised Riemann hypothesis (GRH), which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers, and could expand our understanding of a broader family of mathematical structures. “There are numerous results that are conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems!” says James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London. “I suppose most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. What is both unsettling and tremendously exciting, is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results. It is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.” Alpöge has been involved in a number of recent discoveries involving AI. In July, he announced that the Jacobian conjecture – which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true – is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof . He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered “stepping stones” to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution . Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after. “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier,” he writes, saying that he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that “there was a constraint to respect” before the announcement could be made.

item.title: ISS astronauts look down on the snow-capped Himalayas | Space photo of the day for Nov. 20, 2026
item.description: null A snapshot of the Himalayas captured from aboard the ISS. (Image credit: CSA/Joshua Kutryk) The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station . What is it? Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space. Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse. This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest. Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4Q November 17, 2026 Why is it incredible? From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission , even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range. It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home. Perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

item.title: US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop
item.description: The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA's effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved. The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic. Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN . Bedford also said that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy plans to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20. Read full article Comments

item.title: Lagos Hosts 2026 International Theatre Festival, Featuring Local and International Productions
item.description: The third edition of the Lagos International Theatre Festival (LITF) has concluded successfully, attracting over 20,000 attendees from November 9 to 15, 2026. Featuring more than 25 productions, international performances from Kenya, Brazil, Norway and Canada, high-profile diplomatic engagements and a spectacular Opening Night Gala, the festival reinforced its growing position as an important platform for showcasing Nigerian creativity and connecting global theatre communities. The impressive turnout, diversity of productions and international participation demonstrated the growing appetite for live theatre and the potential of cultural platforms to stimulate creative enterprise, encourage international collaboration and strengthen Nigeria’s global cultural presence. A Vision For Global Recognition Speaking on the success of the festival, Founder and Creative Producer, Bolanle Austen-Peters , said: “Our ambition has always been to create more than a theatre festival. We want to build a platform that places Lagos firmly on the global cultural map, gives African stories the international visibility they deserve and creates meaningful opportunities for our artists. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and bringing international performers from four countries to Lagos is a powerful affirmation of this vision. Theatre is not just entertainment; it is an instrument of cultural identity, economic opportunity and global influence. The Stage Is Everywhere, and Africa must claim its rightful place on that stage.” A Week Of Culture And Collaboration The festival opened on November 9 with Theatre Meets Food at Kaly Restaurant, featuring celebrated chef Hilda Baci in a unique fusion of culinary artistry and live performance. The week also featured diplomatic and cultural engagements hosted by the United States Consul General in Lagos and the British Embassy, alongside a networking reception organised by the British Council for festival directors and participating production companies. These engagements highlighted the importance of international partnerships and cultural diplomacy in advancing Nigeria’s creative industry. A Celebration Of Excellence A major highlight was the Opening Night Gala, held on November 13 at Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, which welcomed over 1,000 guests, including the Governor of Lagos State, Babajide Olusola Sanwo-Olu ; the Chargé d’Affaires of the US Mission in Nigeria; the US Consul General; the British Deputy High Commissioner; the Consul General of Brazil; the Consul General of South Africa, the Ambassador of the Republic of Korea; alongside other members of the diplomatic corps, heads of institutions, government representatives, international delegates and leading figures in the creative industry. Food, beverage and lifestyle brands also contributed to the festival atmosphere, extending the experience beyond the stage. Reflecting on the achievement, Vanessa Jev, Festival Director, said: “This year’s festival demonstrated what is possible when artistic vision, strong partnerships and collective commitment come together. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and hosting international participants from four countries required months of planning and the dedication of an exceptional team. We are proud to have created a platform where Nigerian and international artists could share their work, connect with new audiences and build lasting relationships. With growing audience engagement, international participation and institutional partnerships, LITF remains committed to showcasing exceptional talent, promoting cultural exchange and building a sustainable global platform for African storytelling. LITF 2026 — THE STAGE IS EVERYWHERE. Through performances, cultural engagements and industry collaborations, LITF promotes artistic excellence, encourages cultural exchange and supports the growth of the performing arts industry, with a vision to position Lagos as a leading theatre destination in Africa. item.title: Microsoft's last non-security preview of 2026 packs a punch
item.description: Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview update of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for users who prefer darker rooms. The optional KB5132057 update arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday. Microsoft is skipping December's non-security preview because of reduced holiday operations, though that doesn't cancel the monthly security release. This last preview is quite a doozy. The big-ticket item is the "new Windows Search Experience." We saw a preview of this last month, and Microsoft has gone well beyond the "just make it work" request of many Windows users. Results appear faster with less clutter, the tool uses memory better, and files can be previewed directly in Windows Search. We're less convinced by inline actions, which let users perform common tasks directly through Windows Search without opening Settings. In our testing, "turn on dark mode" worked, but "switch on dark mode" did not, thus highlighting the limitations of the tool. In addition, we remain unconvinced that Windows Search is the place to run actions. That said, anything that makes Windows Search less of a punchline for unkind jokes about performance and accuracy is welcome, as are other features, including an optional screen-brightening feature for Windows Hello facial recognition in dim rooms, and the PowerToys-esque Run dialog, which users can enable in Settings. While some of the new features won't be enabled immediately, Microsoft has included fixes that will be available right away. One addresses an issue where Windows Fax and Scan could fail to connect to a fax server. Handy for those occasions when email falls over into a heap . There are also fixes for Windows IoT Enterprise LTSC activation failures and the misleading "Something went wrong" message shown on Android devices during cross-device passkey authentication. At the time of writing, Microsoft still lists the problem as something for which "we are working on a resolution to be released in a future Windows update." Sadly, not everything has been pushed off the naughty step. SQL Server queries using OLE DB providers can still leave connections to external databases open after they've finished. Microsoft is working on that one and "will provide an update in an upcoming release." ®

item.title: SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space
item.description: Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers. The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips. SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter. Read full article Comments

item.title: Microsoft suggests Registry hack to work around hotpatch woes
item.description: Some Windows 11 applications might fail to install or launch after Microsoft's November hotpatch, but not to worry: there's a Registry tweak to work around it. Microsoft has confirmed it isn't administrators' imaginations. The November hotpatch is causing application errors, including in little-used and obscure apps such as Outlook. Affected applications may fail during installation, launch, or use, displaying errors such as " ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099) ." Microsoft's investigation points to applications that load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, msi.dll. The problem is more common with 32-bit software, but can also affect 64-bit applications "under certain circumstances." The workaround involves fiddling with the Registry on affected devices, so is not for the faint of heart and a backup is a good idea before diving in. Microsoft says the key " HotPatchTableSize " in the folder " HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management " needs to be set to " 2000 " followed by a restart. Just the thing to round out the week for administrators. The issue affects the November hotpatch, not the standard monthly cumulative security update. "Devices which installed the November 2026 Windows monthly security update are not expected to be affected by this issue," Microsoft said. Windows hotpatches are security updates that don't require a device restart (unless, as in this instance, administrators have to do so to address errors after a hotpatch is installed). Windows 11 hotpatching requires version 24H2 or later, an eligible subscription, and the necessary management and security configuration. "Hotpatch update package size is significantly smaller than the standard cumulative updates," Microsoft said, and the goal is to "streamline the installation process and enhance compliance efficiency." The offending hotpatch, KB5132043 , was released on November 10. It followed the October 13 baseline , which was a prerequisite. Microsoft made hotpatching the default in Windows Autopatch earlier this year. At the time, we asked: " What could possibly go wrong? " Thanks to November's hotpatch, we have our answer. ®

Just the thing to round out the week for administrators. The issue affects the November hotpatch, not the standard monthly cumulative security update. "Devices which installed the November 2026 Windows monthly security update are not expected to be affected by this issue," Microsoft said. Windows hotpatches are security updates that don't require a device restart (unless, as in this instance, administrators have to do so to address errors after a hotpatch is installed). Windows 11 hotpatching requires version 24H2 or later, an eligible subscription, and the necessary management and security configuration. "Hotpatch update package size is significantly smaller than the standard cumulative updates," Microsoft said, and the goal is to "streamline the installation process and enhance compliance efficiency." The offending hotpatch, KB5132043 , was released on November 10. It followed the October 13 baseline , which was a prerequisite. Microsoft made hotpatching the default in Windows Autopatch earlier this year. At the time, we asked: " What could possibly go wrong? " Thanks to November's hotpatch, we have our answer. ®

item.title: Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone
item.description: Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation's most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX showed it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 launches on Vulcan over the next few years. Your faithful correspondents will take a break from the Rocket Report next week for the Thanksgiving holiday, so we'll see you again the first week of December. As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar. Europe's leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker . Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company, Ars reports . Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, with a valuation of more than $12 billion after the company's most recent fundraising round in June. Read full article Comments

item.title: I got to tour SpaceX's Starfactory facility in Starbase, Texas, and what I saw blew my mind
item.description: null STARBASE, Texas — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless. The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies. For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity. Inside Starfactory We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us. Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener. The exterior of SpaceX's Starfactory facility at Starbase, Texas. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Future) Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close). Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how big the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare. item.dc:creator: Josh Dinner
item.content:encoded: null STARBASE, Texas — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless. The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies. For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity. Inside Starfactory We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us. Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener. The exterior of SpaceX's Starfactory facility at Starbase, Texas. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Future) Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close). Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how big the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare. Starbase, Texas https://t.co/NqDWwUZXv9 August 25, 2025 As our tour continued and we passed rows of nose cones under preparation for integration, numbering as high as Ship 51, one stood out from the others. In the distance, only visible for moment between the overlapping views of other Ships as we walked through the production stations, was a nose cone with a series of windows cut out of its face - undoubtedly a prototype for, or possibly even the final article that will be used as NASA's Artemis lunar lander. NASA has contracted SpaceX to develop a version of Starship capable of landing astronauts on the moon as a part of the agency's Artemis program, and this appeared to the Ship being readied for when that mission arrives. NASA is targeting Artemis IV as the program's first crewed lunar landing in 2028, and while the decision solidifying Starship as the lander tasked with that mission isn't finalized (Blue Origin is also vying for that spot with its Blue Moon lander), SpaceX is clearly operating with the intention of coming out ahead. But Artemis is clearly not SpaceX's only focus, as evident by the many, many other Ships in production that did not have window holes carved out of them.SpaceX officials said the company is currently completing about one Ship upper stage every two weeks, and one Super Heavy booster every four weeks, with overlapping production allowing multiple rockets to move through the factory simultaneously. The majority of the vehicles currently being assembled will carry stacks of SpaceX's upgraded Starlink Version 3 (V3) satellites. A photo of a Starship rocket upright in a hangar at Starfactory, shared by U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth via social media . (Image credit: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth via X) The company's Starlink network in low Earth orbit currently consists of more than 11,000 spacecraft beaming wireless internet to SpaceX customers across the globe. All of those were launched on SpaceX's workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, with the exception of a few more than 50 delivered on Starship's two most recent test flights. Both carried V3 Starlink stacks to add to the constellation, which SpaceX officials say each added the data capacity equivalent to ten Falcon 9 Starlink launches. And, as they fine tune Starship's design, SpaceX plans to increase the vehicle's launch cadence dramatically, growing the Starlink network as it does. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has stated the company hopes to launch Starship about once a week beginning in 2027, and with the number of Ships we saw lined up inside Starfactory, launch vehicle inventory doesn't seem like it will be to blame if that goal isn't realized. Building rockets like cars (and Lego bricks) SpaceX has adopted a manufacturing process modeled after the automotive industry, where efficiency and reproduction allow for the manufacture of large numbers of identical parts. Automation is a critical part of that process, but not one SpaceX is ready to entirely rely on. Much of the equipment and tools being used for Starship's production were designed by SpaceX engineers, who are constantly refining production processes to eliminate bottlenecks. And SpaceX has deliberately kept technicians on the floor as Starship's design continues to evolve, rather than automating procedures that might soon become obsolete. Our tour guide compared SpaceX's manufacturing consistency goals to that of Lego bricks, which are famously precise in their production down to the micro-millimeter accuracy of what now number more than 1 trillion bricks made since the toy company began in the 1940s. Expansion Exiting the far side of the building, we stood in the shadow of SpaceX's two towering Mega Bays, where the sections of Starship are stacked and integrated with their engines - there's one hanger for Ship, and another for Super Heavy. Each can hold about five or six assemblies, and housed two or three vehicles at the time our tour was brought by. Both Mega Bays, however, looked small against the adjacent Gigabay SpaceX is currently constructing. At approximately 700,000 square feet (65,000 square meters), Gigabay will be equipped with room to accommodate up to 24 vehicles at a time, and will facilitate a major increase in SpaceX's ability to assemble its Ship and Super Heavy rockets. Part of SpaceX's goal with Starship is to make all of what we got to see completely routine; to make rocket launches and landings as ordinary as commercial airline flights. Still, standing inside Starfactory, surrounded on all sides by huge spacecraft in various stages of assembly, it was hard to imagine a reality where giant rockets flying to and from space on a regular basis wouldn't feel like science fiction. Later that day a giant rocket launched to outer space - Super Heavy did attempt a return to pad, but was diverted for an offshore landing instead, where it exploded. But the next day, Ship 42 came plunging through the overcast cloud cover, falling belly-first toward the same tower it left just a couple dozen hours before. And then it lit its engines and was caught by the tower. That felt like science fiction too.

item.title: AI could open wallets where ERP upgrade pitches can't, says PwC
item.description: Global consultancy PwC says IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch. The Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier. Selling that prospect, rather than incremental improvements to existing processes, could help IT leaders justify a migration. Oracle and SAP are both trying to persuade customers to move from established ERP systems to newer platforms. For SAP, that means S/4HANA, preferably in the cloud. For Oracle, it means Fusion Cloud Applications. Moving from ECC or E-Business Suite, respectively, can involve root-and-branch changes to technology and business processes, rather than a straightforward software upgrade. Thousands of organizations still rely on these aging, often heavily customized systems. IT leaders struggle to justify a costly, time-consuming migration when the reward appears to be doing the same meat-and-veg business processes slightly better. For example, a survey of SAP users last year found that 95 percent said building a positive case for migration required substantial effort or was genuinely challenging. Speaking to The Register , Jennifer Colapietro, PwC digital core modernization platform leader, said: "You're seeing it a lot more as part of the rationale for the business case for why they should upgrade, answering the question: 'Why now? What should we prioritize?' Certainly, AI and getting the value of AI, a key business case justification for that. "Folks have budgets for ERP, but now [funding for transformation is] being split because they also have budgets for AI. But there's synergies across them. If you look at moving to a clean digital core ERP, that will help them to realize the AI value faster... be able to turn on AI and be able to start to automate a lot of the processes and implement the agents. That helps to build the business case." SAP recently introduced Joule 2.0 while Oracle has announced Fusion Claw . With both of these new technologies, the vendors are promising customers they can build AI agents to automate business processes and perform some work that was previously done by humans. Colapietro argued that moving to more modern platforms makes deploying AI agents easier and more effective than adding AI capabilities around legacy systems. "It is more challenging to apply AI to the older systems. We focus on the importance of a clean digital core as the foundation for getting the value and effectiveness out of AI and scaling AI responsibly. I think that's given," she said. An ERP replacement isn't the only route to AI, however. We focus on the importance of a clean digital core as the foundation for getting the value and effectiveness out of AI and scaling AI responsibly. I think that's given," she said. European home improvement retailer Kingfisher – which owns the B&Q brand in the UK – eschewed SAP's overtures to upgrade its ECC system, despite encroaching deadlines. Mainstream maintenance for supported ECC 6.0 versions ends in December 2027, with optional extended maintenance through 2030 at a premium of two percentage points on the existing maintenance base. Kingfisher opted instead for third-party support from Rimini Street , building an AI strategy around its existing ERP system using a combination of technology from Databricks and Google. AI might help sell an ERP migration to the board. It doesn't make replacing the ERP system a prerequisite. ®

item.title: Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings
item.description: Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate . This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes , some of which are challenging prediction markets , while others are trying to get in on the action themselves. In the new lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal" in Florida. Read full article Comments

item.title: Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand
item.description: The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security. The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data. The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government. The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters. The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month. A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers. For Apple, a company that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected. While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand. At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens. In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US. Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators. Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless. Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not. What the judgment does not confirm While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public. "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret

While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.
